title: Best MCP Servers and Tools for Claude in 2026: The Definitive Guide
description: We build and run MCP servers in production every day. Here are the best MCP servers for Claude in 2026 — security auditing, accessibility testing, code signing, design systems, and more.
author: Sophie Cave
content:
The Model Context Protocol ecosystem has exploded. As of June 2026, there are thousands of MCP servers in the registry, with millions of monthly SDK downloads. Every major AI tool — Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf — now supports MCP natively.

Most of these servers are wrappers around existing APIs. Some are genuinely useful. A few are transformative. We know because we build MCP servers and use them in production every day at Like One.

This guide covers the MCP servers worth installing in 2026 — organized by what they actually do, not by how many GitHub stars they have.

What Makes an MCP Server Worth Using

Before the list: most MCP servers are not worth your time. The registry is full of thin wrappers that add a tool definition around a single API call. You could make that call yourself in three lines of code.

A good MCP server does one of three things:

  • Gives Claude capabilities it cannot have otherwise — browser automation, visual inspection, hardware access, or domain-specific analysis that requires specialized logic.
  • Encapsulates complex multi-step workflows — security audits, accessibility scans, or deployment pipelines that would take dozens of manual tool calls.
  • Provides persistent context — memory systems, knowledge bases, or project-specific data that survives across conversations.

If an MCP server just wraps a REST API with no additional logic, skip it. Claude can call APIs directly.

Security and Code Quality

MCP Shield — Security Auditing for MCP Servers

MCP Shield scans MCP server code for security vulnerabilities before you install them. It checks for prompt injection vectors, unsafe tool patterns, credential exposure, and twenty other security rules.

Why it matters: every MCP server you install gets access to your AI agent's tool-calling capabilities. A malicious or poorly written server can exfiltrate data, execute arbitrary commands, or manipulate your agent's behavior through prompt injection. MCP Shield catches these issues before they become problems.

Install it. Run it on every new MCP server before you add it to your configuration. This is non-negotiable security hygiene.

Orchard Sign — Apple Code Signing Diagnostics

Orchard Sign is an MCP server that diagnoses and fixes Apple code signing issues. It understands provisioning profiles, entitlements, certificate chains, and the dozens of ways Xcode signing can break.

If you ship iOS or macOS apps with Claude Code, this server turns cryptic signing errors into actionable fixes. It recognizes forty-four distinct error patterns and provides specific remediation steps for each one.

Orchard HIG — Apple Human Interface Guidelines Checker

Orchard HIG checks your UI code against Apple's Human Interface Guidelines. It validates spacing, typography, color contrast, touch targets, and navigation patterns against the official design specifications.

This is not a linter. It is a design system validator that understands context. It knows the difference between a primary action button that needs 44-point touch targets and a toolbar icon that follows different rules.

Accessibility

TechAccess — AI-Native Accessibility Testing

TechAccess combines axe-core scanning, Playwright ARIA extraction, and AI analysis to audit websites for WCAG compliance. It does not just find violations — it generates alt text, analyzes semantic structure, and produces code remediation with before-and-after diffs.

The accessibility testing market is projected to reach nearly two billion dollars in 2026. Most tools in this space scan for violations and hand you a report. TechAccess scans, diagnoses, and fixes. That auto-remediation capability is the differentiator.

It supports multi-page crawling with sitemap discovery, so you can audit an entire site in a single command. The HTML dashboard gives you a visual overview of scores across every page.

Axe MCP Server (Deque)

Deque recently launched their official axe MCP Server, bringing their industry-standard accessibility scanning engine directly into Claude and Cursor. If you already use axe-core in your CI pipeline, this gives your AI agent native access to the same scanning capabilities.

The limitation: it scans but does not fix. You get violation reports, but remediation is still manual. For teams that need automated fixes, you will need to pair it with a remediation tool or use something like TechAccess that handles both.

Memory and Knowledge

Claude Brain — Persistent Memory for Claude

Claude Brain gives Claude persistent memory across conversations. It stores context as key-value entries with semantic search, so your AI agent can remember decisions, preferences, project state, and anything else that matters between sessions.

We use this as the backbone of our entire agent memory system. Every session boots by reading brain state. Every important decision gets written back. The result is an AI that actually knows your project, your preferences, and your history.

If you are building any kind of persistent AI system, you need a memory layer. Claude Brain is one approach. The key insight is that memory should be structured and searchable, not just a dump of conversation logs.

Filesystem and Database Servers

The official Anthropic filesystem MCP server gives Claude read and write access to specified directories. The PostgreSQL and SQLite servers let Claude query databases directly. These are foundational — not exciting, but essential for any serious development workflow.

The filesystem server is particularly useful when combined with Claude Code's built-in file tools, because it lets you define precise access boundaries. You can give Claude access to your source code directory without exposing your entire home folder.

Visual and Frontend

LO Eyes — Visual Frontend Inspector

LO Eyes takes screenshots, scans for visual issues, and audits frontend layouts. It uses Playwright to render pages across device sizes and identify problems that are invisible in code — broken layouts, overlapping elements, incorrect responsive behavior.

This solves a fundamental limitation of text-based AI tools: they cannot see your UI. LO Eyes gives Claude actual visual context, so it can identify and fix layout issues that would otherwise require a human to spot.

Browserbase and Playwright Servers

Several MCP servers provide browser automation capabilities. Browserbase offers cloud-hosted browser instances with anti-detection features. The Playwright MCP server gives Claude direct control of a local browser for testing and scraping.

For web development workflows, browser automation is essential. Your AI agent needs to see the result of its code changes. These servers close the loop between writing code and verifying it works.

Development and DevOps

GitHub MCP Server

The official GitHub MCP server lets Claude create issues, manage pull requests, review code, and interact with repositories. Combined with Claude Code, this creates a complete development workflow where your AI agent can write code, create a branch, open a PR, and respond to review comments.

This is one of the most mature MCP servers available. If you use GitHub, install it.

Vercel and Deployment Servers

The Vercel MCP server lets Claude deploy projects, check deployment status, view build logs, and manage domains. Similar servers exist for other platforms.

The value here is closing the deployment loop. Instead of Claude Code writing code and then waiting for you to deploy it manually, the agent can deploy, verify the deployment succeeded, and even check runtime logs for errors. This is what agentic loops look like in practice.

Docker and Infrastructure Servers

Docker MCP servers let Claude manage containers, build images, and orchestrate services. For teams running containerized development environments, this means Claude can spin up test databases, run integration tests against real services, and clean up after itself.

Data and Research

Web Search and Fetch Servers

Several MCP servers add web search and page fetching capabilities. Brave Search, Exa, and Tavily each offer different approaches — traditional search, neural search, and research-optimized retrieval respectively.

For RAG systems and research workflows, these are essential. Your AI agent needs access to current information that is not in its training data.

Database Servers

PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and Supabase MCP servers let Claude query and modify databases directly. The Supabase server is particularly well-integrated, supporting migrations, edge functions, and full project management.

Be careful with write permissions. Give your AI agent read access to production databases for debugging. Save write access for development and staging environments.

Communication

Slack, Email, and Calendar Servers

Slack MCP servers let Claude read channels, send messages, and manage threads. Gmail servers handle email. Google Calendar servers manage scheduling. These turn Claude into an autonomous assistant that can communicate on your behalf.

The risk with communication servers is obvious: an AI sending messages as you. Use these with explicit approval workflows. Most implementations support draft mode, where Claude prepares messages for your review before sending.

How to Evaluate an MCP Server Before Installing

The MCP ecosystem is moving fast, and not every server in the registry deserves your trust. Here is our evaluation checklist:

  1. Read the source code. Every MCP server runs with the permissions of your AI agent. If you would not install a random npm package without reading it, do not install a random MCP server either.
  2. Check for security issues. Run MCP Shield or manually review for credential handling, input validation, and command injection vectors.
  3. Test in isolation. Run new servers in a sandbox environment before adding them to your production workflow.
  4. Verify maintenance. Check commit history and issue response times. Abandoned servers accumulate security debt.
  5. Assess scope. Does the server request more permissions than it needs? A weather server should not need filesystem access.

Beyond the checklist, understand how MCP servers execute in your environment. Most servers run as child processes spawned by your AI client. They inherit your user permissions, can access your filesystem, and can make network requests. A compromised server is not sandboxed — it has the same access as any application you run. Configure servers with minimal filesystem paths, restrict network access where possible, and never run MCP servers with elevated privileges.

Supply chain risk is real. MCP servers depend on npm or pip packages, each introducing its own dependency tree. A single compromised dependency can turn a legitimate server into an attack vector. Pin your dependencies, audit transitive packages, and prefer servers with minimal dependency footprints. The simpler the server, the smaller the attack surface.

Building Your MCP Stack

You do not need every server on this list. Start with what solves your immediate problems:

  • Every developer: GitHub + filesystem + one database server + MCP Shield for security
  • Web developers: Add a browser automation server + LO Eyes for visual testing + TechAccess for accessibility
  • iOS/macOS developers: Add Orchard Sign + Orchard HIG
  • Teams: Add Slack + deployment server + Claude Brain for shared context

The servers that deliver the most value are the ones that close loops in your workflow — turning multi-step manual processes into single tool calls that your AI agent handles autonomously.

As your stack grows, organization matters. Group servers by function in your configuration. Document why each server is installed and what it replaces. Review your active servers quarterly — remove any you have not used in the last month. Every unused server is unnecessary attack surface and wasted startup time. The best MCP stack is the smallest one that covers your actual workflow.

The MCP Ecosystem in 2026

MCP adoption has accelerated beyond early predictions. The protocol has become the standard for extending AI capabilities, supported by every major AI coding tool and a growing number of enterprise platforms.

The opportunity for developers is clear: building MCP servers is one of the highest-leverage skills in AI development right now. Every custom server you build gives your AI agent a new capability that directly translates to productivity.

For teams evaluating MCP adoption, start with security and developer tools. These categories deliver measurable value from day one — fewer manual reviews, faster deployments, and automated compliance checks. Communication and research servers are powerful but carry higher risk due to their ability to send messages and access external data on your behalf.

The ecosystem will keep growing. The servers worth using will be the ones that solve real problems with real logic — not thin API wrappers. Choose carefully, audit aggressively, and build what does not exist yet.

faqs.question: What is an MCP server?
faqs.answer: An MCP (Model Context Protocol) server is a program that gives AI models like Claude access to external tools and data. It defines tools that the AI can call — like reading files, querying databases, taking screenshots, or running security scans. MCP servers run locally or remotely and communicate with AI clients through a standardized protocol.

faqs.question: How do I install an MCP server for Claude?
faqs.answer: Add the server configuration to your Claude Code settings file (usually .mcp.json in your project root or ~/.claude/mcp.json globally). Each server needs a command to start it and optional environment variables. Claude Code will automatically start the server and make its tools available in your session.

faqs.question: Are MCP servers safe to use?
faqs.answer: MCP servers run with whatever permissions you grant them, so you should treat them like any other software you install. Read the source code before installing, run security scanning tools like MCP Shield, and test new servers in isolation before adding them to production workflows. Never install servers from untrusted sources without review.

faqs.question: What is the best MCP server for security?
faqs.answer: MCP Shield is specifically designed to audit MCP servers for security vulnerabilities. It checks for prompt injection vectors, credential exposure, unsafe command execution, and twenty other security patterns. Run it on every new MCP server before you install it.

faqs.question: Can MCP servers work with Cursor and other AI tools?
faqs.answer: Yes. MCP is an open standard supported by Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and other AI development tools. Any MCP server that follows the protocol specification will work with any compatible client. The configuration format may differ slightly between tools.

faqs.question: How many MCP servers should I install?
faqs.answer: Install only what you need. Each server adds startup time and memory usage. Start with three to five servers that solve your most common workflow gaps — typically a filesystem server, a version control server, and one or two domain-specific tools. Add more as specific needs arise.

faqs.question: What is the difference between MCP servers and Claude Code built-in tools?
faqs.answer: Claude Code includes built-in tools for file reading, editing, bash commands, and web searching. MCP servers extend these capabilities with specialized tools — browser automation, database queries, deployment, visual inspection, and domain-specific analysis that Claude Code does not handle natively.

faqs.question: Can I build my own MCP server?
faqs.answer: Yes. The MCP SDK is available in Python and TypeScript. A basic MCP server can be built in under an hour. You define tools as functions with typed parameters, and the SDK handles protocol communication. See our guide on building MCP servers from scratch for a complete walkthrough.

faqs.question: Do MCP servers cost money?
faqs.answer: Most open source MCP servers are free. Some cloud-hosted servers (like Browserbase) have usage-based pricing. Official servers from companies like GitHub and Vercel are free but require API tokens for their respective services. Running servers locally has no cost beyond compute resources.

faqs.question: What are the most popular MCP servers in 2026?
faqs.answer: The most widely used MCP servers include the official GitHub server for version control, filesystem servers for file access, database servers for PostgreSQL and SQLite, browser automation servers for web testing, and Slack servers for team communication. Specialized servers for security auditing, accessibility testing, and code signing are growing rapidly in adoption.
